nameStory: The maple spanworm moth gets its name from its caterpillar, which feeds on maple trees and moves like a classic "spanworm" or "inchworm" — arching its body into loops as it crawls along branches. The "spanworm" name comes from this distinctive way of measuring distances by "spanning" with its body, like using your hand span to measure something.
description: The maple spanworm moth is a medium-sized moth that's a master of disguise, perfectly mimicking a dead autumn leaf when at rest. With wings spanning nearly 2 inches across, it displays beautiful orange, brown, and yellow tones that would blend seamlessly into a pile of fallen maple leaves. This nocturnal moth flies from summer through late fall, spending its days resting motionless against tree bark or building walls where its camouflage makes it nearly invisible. It's part of the geometer moth family, known for their caterpillars that "measure" the earth as they walk.

idTips.label: Leaf-like appearance
idTips.description: When wings are closed, looks exactly like a dried autumn leaf with irregular edges and mottled brown, orange, and tan coloring that feels papery to the touch

idTips.label: Notched wing edges
idTips.description: Wing margins have distinctive irregular scallops and notches, not smooth like many other moths, giving them that authentic dead-leaf silhouette

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wings spanning about 1.5-2.5 inches across, roughly the size of a large maple or oak leaf

idTips.label: Resting position
idTips.description: Holds wings vertically above body like a butterfly when resting, rather than spread horizontally like most moths, enhancing the dead-leaf illusion

idTips.label: Color variation
idTips.description: Ranges from bright orange-yellow to deep rusty brown, often with darker lines and spots that mimic leaf veins and decay spots

idTips.label: Nighttime activity
idTips.description: Comes to lights at night during summer and fall, but during day remains perfectly still and can be surprisingly difficult to spot even when you know it's there

habitat: Found throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests, especially areas rich in maples, oaks, birches, and other hardwood trees that their caterpillars feed on. You'll encounter adults around porch lights, building walls, and tree trunks in suburban areas as well as deep woods. They're equally at home in lowland forests and mountain slopes up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Not active during spring months. Pupae are developing underground or in leaf litter, preparing for summer emergence.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin emerging in July and can be found at lights or resting on buildings and trees during the day. Peak activity occurs on warm, humid nights.
seasonality.fall: Continues flying through October and into early November, with the latest individuals still active during warm autumn nights. Their leaf-like appearance is perfect camouflage among actual fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but eggs laid in fall will overwinter to hatch as caterpillars the following spring.

funFact: This moth's camouflage is so perfect that even when you're staring directly at one resting on a tree trunk or building wall during the day, your brain often refuses to register it as anything other than a stuck leaf — until it suddenly flies away and startles you!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with actual dead leaves when resting during the day, which is exactly what the moth wants! Other autumn-colored moths like the cecropia or promethea have much larger, rounder wings without the irregular notched edges. Remember: if that "leaf" on the wall has perfectly symmetrical "damage" on both sides, it's probably a maple spanworm moth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the "maple" spanworm moth, its caterpillars actually feed on a wide variety of trees including oak, birch, elm, ash, and basswood — basically any deciduous tree in the forest. The maple association likely stuck because these are such common and noticeable host trees.
compareHints: The maple spanworm moth is the only Ennomos species commonly found in New England, making identification easier within its genus. Compared to other geometer moths in the region, it's distinguished by its larger size, pronounced leaf-like appearance, and the distinctive notched wing edges that give it one of its alternate names — the "notched wing moth."
